pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/59629

This is mainly superseding https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/62509 now that the APIs have been approved. I have addressed most of the comments from @stephentoub  there except for two things which I plan to do in this PR by adding one more commit which are:
- [x] Implement Regex.Run<TState> on top of Regex.Run in order to avoid duplication.
- [x] For most of the tests where we are testing isMatch with string, also call in the isMatch(span) new methods to get test coverage into the new surface area.

While I add the above two bullets into a commit, I thought of pushing this PR as it is ready for review other than those two things.

issue_context.title: Augment Regex extensibility point for better perf and span-based matching
comments:
@jeffhandley, this would be a good issue for someone as a way to ramp up on S.T.RE while also accomplishing several impactful results. It could be split into a handful of PRs, each moving the ball forward, e.g.

PRs:
1. Update the engines to read base.runtext once at the beginning of `FindFirstChar` and `Go`, `AsSpan()` it into a local,  and then all reads of the text should be via that local for the rest of the method.  All engines could be done together, or one PR each. No test changes should be needed.  At that point, the implementations are all span-based, and everything else is hooking stuff up.

2. (Optional) Update the implementations to slice that span once upfront based on runtextend (and possibly runtextbeg, though that could complicate some other things around the exact indices returned for matches), and then all subsequent checks can be based on the span length instead of runtextend (and maybe 0 instead of runtextbeg). The primary goal would be cleaning up the implementation a bit and helping perf by removing bounds checks in some cases on the span accesses.  This would help highlight benefits of using span internally, but is not strictly necessary for the rest of the work.

3. Refactor the existing `Scan` loop into an internal virtual method that looks like the one we'd want to expose as protected.

4. Override that new virtual on each of the engines,  other than in the source generator, which would require the functionality be exposed publicly. This could be one PR per engine or one all-up. This should include changing the existing `FindFirstChar`/`Go` overrides to be non-virtual and accept the input span from the `Scan` loop; the abstract methods can then be temporarily overridden with methods that just throw `NotSupportedException`.

At this point, the internal implementations should be able to fully support span inputs (which can't be passed in yet), and it should be trivial to prototype the public surface area in order to confirm it works and get it approved.  At which point...

4. Make `FindFirstChar`/`Go` virtual.

5. Expose the new protected surface area and update the source generator to target it, overriding `Scan` instead of `FindFirstChar`/`Go` as was done with the other internal engines. 

6. Add the new public `IsMatch` methods taking spans. 

7. Add the new public `Enumerate` methods. 

8. (Optional) With one PR per interpreter,  compiled,  and source generator,  update the implementations to combine `FindFirstChar`/`Go` into a single method,  rather than being a loop that calls both.  The goal here is perf, and in the case of the source generator,  easier to understand code flow for someone reading/debugging the generated source.

Small question about the new static APIs: should they add several overloads (to stay consistent with the old API) or would it be better to add just one overload with optional parameters (to make the API simpler and easier to understand)?

> Small question about the new static APIs: should they add several overloads (to stay consistent with the old API) or would it be better to add just one overload with optional parameters (to make the API simpler and easier to understand)?

TimeSpan's can't be optional, and the TimeSpan matchTimeout should be at the end to be consistent with all the other methods; it could be made nullable, but that then introduces multiple values for infinite, which I don't love.  Combine that with a desire for consistency across all the APIs, and my preference is to use multiple overloads instead of optional parameters here.  But it's something that can be discussed in API review.

>protected virtual void Scan(ReadOnlySpan<char> text);

Regarding this API suggestion, I suppose you meant `protected internal virtual...` instead of just `protected` right? If not, then it isn't possible to call it from the Regex.Run method.

> I suppose you meant protected internal virtual

Yes. (I left out the internal part as it's an implementation detail and not part of the public signature.)

>but today this one is reused for doing Match.NextMatch() on the Match object returned

Looks like I got confused a bit and I was wrong about this assumption. That said, I did see that runmatch is not always set back to null after running Scan, for example, when `quick` is true (meaning when just doing `IsMatch()` and not actually returning Match to caller):

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1996f3d0179bbe3464b7d47e185008bfae4d9326/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/RegexRunner.cs#L190-L194

As well as when using Split/Replace:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1996f3d0179bbe3464b7d47e185008bfae4d9326/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/RegexRunner.cs#L308-L313

In those cases, runmatch will be kept alive and reused and simply just reset to the right positions using:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1996f3d0179bbe3464b7d47e185008bfae4d9326/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/RegexRunner.cs#L452-L462

This may mean that it is ok for us to reuse since it will never be handed out to caller, so I will continue the prototype to see if it can be reused or if we would need the additional protected field in order to not break an existing scenario.
I have updated the top level proposal and factored out the `Enumerate` method for now. The proposed APIs have been prototyped in the following draft PR: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/62509

review_comments: I think you said you're going to rewrite this in this PR, so I'll hold off on reviewing it. #Resolved
Code coverage suggests this is never invoked.  Are we missing tests?

Subsequently, as part of https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/62573, I do think we should consider obsoleting these methods and just making them throw PlatformNotSupportedException.  We don't use them, the docs state "This API supports the product infrastructure and is not intended to be used directly from your code.", and the docs also state "Used by a Regex object generated by the CompileToAssembly method." which simply isn't true.
In the meantime, though, please add at least one test to make sure things aren't totally busted.  We should either validate that the API is functional or PNSE it.
It'd be good to add some simple tests that confirm these throw NIE.
Same question
Nit: can you add an XML comment to this that highlights the difference from Match.Success?
We don't need to null out runtext as was previously being done?
That said, this method is tiny and there's little-to-no customization of it.  The function could just be deleted and its code moved into the call site.

Yeah, I believe this is what I was suggesting offline, the only customization is whether or not we should call CheckTimeout depending on if there is one or not. If we prefer to not have to generate one more method, I'm fine with keeping Scan inside regex dll and only emit FFC and Go (with new names) for now. This is how I originally had it but I believe you asked to instead move to generate Scan instead in favor of a future move away from the FFC/Go design.
I very well may have :)  It's fine as-is.
Why don't we need to do any of this in the span-based Run overload?

We will eventually, but we don't for `IsMatch`. What I did in this PR is basically the minimum to support isMatch overload which basically is: return null if you found a match, and Match.Empty otherwise. I plan to add the rest of the body of this method when I add Count, Enumerate, etc.
Ok. FWIW, that makes it harder to review that it's doing the right thing, since it's obviously not for the coming functionality.

Subsequently I'm really tempted to go and delete all of these "macros".  I don't know that they bring a lot of value, and frequently evolving the code means we end up adding and removing them based on the exact opcodes required.

In my opinion they do tend to make the code slightly easier to read, and also it makes our code look closer to the IL on a regular assembly so I don't mind them. I'm not opposed to removing them either, but I wouldn't be opposed to keep them either.
Don't these changes break the behavior of this protected method? e.g. it's no longer setting the fields based on these values, it's no longer validating the timeout, etc.?

It does, if somebody was manually overriding this Scan method (which AFAIK the answer is nobody) they could end up setting the timeout and all of the rest of the fields twice, as tehy would have been set already via InitializeForScan and they would be resetting them.
This method isn't virtual.  I'm not asking about someone overriding it, but about someone calling it.

Oh right, sorry misunderstood your comment. Yes you are right, this is for sure breaking people directly calling this with values since pretty much all of the parameters now are thrown away essentially. If you think that there are potential consumers calling this, I could just replay the logic of re-setting the values inside this method body (with the added cost that there would be a small perf hit on CompiledToAssembly scenarios).

I expect there's close to 0 users of this, but as it stands they'd all be broken, so we should fix it unless we explicitly choose to break it, in which case we should obsolete it and make it throw PNSE. At the same time, we don't _need_ to call this method ourselves, so if you're concerned about overhead, you can call to an internal method that this also uses. It's not virtual so there are no concerns about using an override.

Technically we probably can't assume runmatch is non-null here, since a derived runner could have set it to null.  I don't think I care, though, since there's a lot of things a RegexRunner could do that will result in null refs. Just calling it out.
I can still adjust the condition and also return null when runmatch is null.

This is clever. I hadn't comprehended what you were doing here before, but you're basically assuming (validly) that the span will always be a subset of the string, and you're using that to recreate the original runtextbeg and runtextend values without complicating the 99.99% case to store them earlier. Nice. A more detailed comment about that would be helpful.

yeah the idea was to not require to pass in runtextbeg and runtextend everytime but now that I look at it again, it won't work in all cases so I think I'll have to rewrite this. The scenario where this won't work is if I do something like:

```c#
myPrecompiledRegex.Match("Some string that has many words but I only want to test the second one", beginning: 5, length: 6);
```

the slice would only be the word `string`, but when I calculate beginning I will be incorrectly setting it to be the last 6 characters `nd one`.  I can see two possible solutions to this, one is to pass in runtextbeg every time, or the other is to special case precompiled scenario (which is the only one that cares about original runtextbeg and end) where it calls back into a new internal property in RegexRunner where we previously save the value during Run().

I know I previously said you didn't need to pass beginning here, but I think you may need to.  The base Scan virtual implementation (that should only be used with legacy CompileToAssembly implementations) is doing this:
```C#
            string? s = runtext;
            if (text != s) throw new Exception(...);
```
If beginning isn't 0, that's going to fail erroneously, because the span won't match the runtext.  I think you'll need to store beginning into runtextbeg, and then in that base method do something like `if (s is not null && s.AsSpan(runtextbeg, runtextend) != text) throw new Exception(...)`, or something along those lines.  And augment the test we have for a precompiled assembly to try different ways of matching... today it's only calling Match, and it's not using any overloads other than the ones that just take a string:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c3f57277b178e11d3a2b495bcff5888b61db1f5c/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/tests/PrecompiledRegexScenarioTest.cs#L23-L25 #Resolved
Good catch, this was indeed broken for the other overloads with the precompiled scenario. I have fixed that and added some overload checks into that same test.
It'd be good to test Matches as well to ensure we get back multiple matches properly, to help validate state is being set appropriately between matches.  #Resolved

Can you also add use of Replace, Split, and Count, since those go through different code paths from IsMatch/Match/Matches? #Resolved

Code coverage suggests that the null case is never exercised.  If it's invalid by construction, we can instead assert it's not null.  If it's potentially hittable but our tests just don't, we should add tests.

Doesn't need to be now, but we might consider deleting the above `if ((uint)length > (uint)input.Length)` check, as this `input.AsSpan(beginning, length)` is also going to validate the length (albeith the error message probably won't be as specific).
